name: Ear stretching

card.summary: Gradually enlarging an earlobe piercing so it can hold plugs, tunnels and other larger jewelry as a visible style and cultural marker.
card.aka: Gauges, gauging, earlobe stretching, flesh tunnels
card.note: Stretching too fast can cause a blowout, with scarring; large stretches rarely close fully without surgery.

quick.overview:
Ear stretching is the deliberate enlargement of a healed piercing, most often in the earlobe, so that it can hold larger jewelry such as plugs, tunnels, claws or spirals. The enlarged lobe and its jewelry are the visible look.

The practice is thousands of years old, documented from the Iceman Otzi (about 3300 BC) to Egyptian, Maasai, Mursi and Aztec traditions, and in modern body-modification and subculture style.
quick.how: Practitioners enlarge a healed piercing gradually in size steps, with jewelry in materials such as steel, titanium or glass. Described methods include inserting the next size, taping, and tapering, and the faster methods are discouraged by piercing guidance.
quick.risks: Stretching too quickly or too far can cause a blowout, where tissue is pushed out of the piercing, leaving scarring. A stretched lobe may shrink somewhat if jewelry is removed, but a hole of about 8 mm (0g) or larger rarely closes to standard size, and surgical repair is the way to close it fully.

lead: Ear stretching is the deliberate enlargement of a healed piercing so it can hold larger jewelry.[1] Earlobes are the most commonly stretched site, followed by septum, tongue and lip piercings, and cartilage is harder to stretch.[1]

People use it to wear plugs, flesh tunnels and similar jewelry, as a style choice and as part of body modification. It also has a long cultural history: Otzi the Iceman (about 3300 BC) had stretched lobes of roughly 7 to 11 mm, and stretched ears appear among the Maasai, Mursi, Lahu and Karen-Padaung peoples and in Aztec, Maya and Moche societies.[1]

chain: Healed piercing is enlarged in steps
Larger plugs or tunnels are worn
angle.text: The stretched lobe and its jewelry are themselves the aesthetic, worn as a style statement or cultural marker. Piercing guidance describes gradual stretching in healed tissue as the lower-risk approach.

infobox: Surgical earlobe repair for large stretches[1]

paras: Described methods include dead stretching (inserting the next larger size), tapering with a lubricated cone, taping with layers of non-adhesive tape, and weighting, which is rarely used now because of migration and tissue thinning.[1] Scalpeling and dermal punching are cutting methods used for some larger or cartilage sites.[1] Piercing guidance generally treats dead stretching as the safest and discourages forcing jewelry or tapering past small sizes.[1]

Plugs, flesh tunnels, ear weights, claws and spirals are common. Non-porous materials such as implant-grade steel, titanium and glass are recommended for fresh stretches, whereas porous materials such as wood, bone, stone and acrylic can trap bacteria.[1] Silicone plugs are not recommended because of their porous, tacky surface.[1]

Stretched ears have been recorded across continents: Otzi (about 3300 BC), Egyptian mummies with plugs over 6 cm, moai statues on Easter Island, the Maasai and Fulani in Africa, the Mursi of Ethiopia, Asian hill tribes, and Aztec, Maya and Moche men in the Americas. Christopher Columbus recorded stretched ears among the Taino in the 1490s.[1]

Stretching too fast or too far can cause a blowout, in which the fistula is pushed out of the piercing, potentially leaving permanent scarring and complicating later stretching or downsizing.[1] A stretched piercing may shrink without jewelry, but results vary, and earlobe repair surgery is the only way to fully close a stretched fistula. A hole of about 0g (8 mm) or larger rarely closes to a standard size.[1]

timeline.event: Otzi the Iceman has stretched lobes of about 7-11 mm.[1]
Columbus records Taino people with stretched ears.[1]
